title: Agreeing on one leader
summary: A leader needs a safe election and a way to stop old owners from acting.

steps.title: Two schedulers both think they own the job
steps.text: A scheduler pauses for twenty seconds. Its lease expires, so another scheduler takes over. The first wakes and sends an invoice anyway. A lease can tell the service who should own a job. It cannot stop a paused process from using an old decision. Choosing one leader and enforcing that choice are separate parts of the design.

steps.title: Raft in plain words
steps.text: Stop the leader and run an election. A term needs a majority of the fixed voter set. Try writes on a partition before and after electing its majority.

steps.title: Worked example: a five-node split
steps.text: Five voters need three. In a 3 versus 2 partition, the three can elect and commit; the two cannot. With a 2 versus 2 versus 1 split, nobody can commit. Two majorities always share a voter, but persistent voting and log rules are what make that intersection useful. An isolated old leader can still believe it is leader in an older term. It must not serve unsafe reads or issue unfenced effects. The game does not model Raft terms or logs, so this example is arithmetic, not a live election.

rows.label: Three voters
rows.how: Tolerates one unavailable voter; often enough

rows.label: Fencing boundary
rows.how: Durably compare tokens where the side effect is accepted

steps.q: Five fixed Raft voters split into groups of three and two. What can the two-node side promise without contacting the other side?
choices: Latest reads from its previously elected leader, while pausing writes
New commits after both surviving voters agree on a higher term
Only explicitly stale reads; majority operations must wait or fail
steps.why: Two voters cannot form a majority of five. An old leader cannot infer current authority from local state.

steps.q: We have a majority election. How could we still send an invoice twice? Follow-up: the provider does not accept fencing tokens.
checklist: Show how a paused old leader can still call the invoice provider
Persist one operation and reuse its provider key across leaders
State what remains ambiguous without provider deduplication
steps.model: A paused old leader can still send a delayed provider call after a new leader takes over. I would fence our local state and persist one invoice intent with an outbox. Every leader and retry reuses the same provider idempotency key. A status lookup helps reconcile, but a negative result alone cannot rule out a request still in flight. Without provider deduplication or another atomic acceptance rule, election alone cannot guarantee exactly one external effect. I would document the duplicate-versus-missing risk and the manual reconciliation path.

steps.title: Make stale ownership harmless
steps.text: An election does not by itself stop an old process from writing to external storage. Advance the term and compare the old token with the storage fence.

steps.q: A worker checks its lease, then pauses. A new owner writes before it resumes. What rejects the delayed old write?
choices: An atomic token comparison and write at the storage resource
Renewing the lease immediately before sending the write
Checking the current token in a separate storage request before writing
steps.why: A separate check leaves another pause window. The receiver must enforce fencing atomically with the effect.

steps.q: Should every request consult the coordination service? Follow-up: its quorum is down for ten minutes.
checklist: Use the coordinator for ownership changes rather than every user request
Specify when cached authority expires and where fencing is enforced
Stop exclusive operations when valid authority cannot be renewed
steps.model: I would cache a versioned owner map and use the coordinator for changes. Existing owners can work only within the protocol's valid authority, with receiver-side fencing. If fresh authority cannot be obtained, operations that require exclusive ownership stop. Public cached reads may continue under a separate promise. Losing a quorum should not silently create two owners. I would consider whether an existing transactional store could own this small decision more simply.

steps.q: SQL already enforces exclusive invoice ownership. Which requirement could justify an additional coordination service?
choices: Electing a worker so provider calls no longer need idempotency
Coordinating ownership of resources outside that database transaction
Caching the SQL owner row so expired ownership is always safe to reuse
steps.why: A separate invariant may need coordination. Election does not deduplicate external effects or make cached authority permanent.

takeaway: Consensus preserves one committed order; fencing carries that authority to the resource.
